faq.q: Why are leaves flat and wide?
faq.a: A flat, wide shape gives a big surface to catch sunlight, and because a leaf is thin, gases and light reach every cell easily. Plants in dry places often have small or needle-shaped leaves to lose less water.

faq.q: What do the veins in a leaf do?
faq.a: Veins are the leaf's plumbing and skeleton. Xylem tubes bring in water and minerals, phloem tubes carry sugar away, and the stiff veins hold the blade open to the light.
Stomata are tiny pores that let carbon dioxide into the leaf and oxygen and water vapour out. A pair of guard cells swells to open each pore and goes floppy to close it.

faq.q: Why is the top of a leaf darker than the bottom?
faq.a: The top has a layer of tall cells packed with chloroplasts, called the palisade layer, to catch the most light. Below is a spongy layer full of air spaces and fewer chloroplasts, so it looks paler.

faq.q: Why do leaves have a waxy coating?
faq.a: The wax, called the cuticle, is waterproof. It stops the leaf losing too much water and helps rain and dirt roll off, while still letting light through.

facts: Most stomata are on the underside of a leaf, where it is shadier and cooler, so less water is lost.
Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots; phloem carries sugars around the plant.
Many leaves have tens of thousands of stomata in each square centimetre of their underside.

quiz.why: Veins contain xylem tubes that carry water from the stem into every part of the leaf.
